andecavi.t: Gallic people of Anjou whose leader Dumnacus fought one of the last campaigns against Rome in 51 BCE.
andecavi.o: The Andecavi, called Andes by Caesar, lived on the lower Loire around Angers. Caesar quartered legions among them in 57 BCE and records that they joined the revolt of 52 BCE.
andecavi.r: Little is known of their institutions beyond their war leaders.
andecavi.e: In 51 BCE Dumnacus besieged the pro-Roman Pictones in Lemonum, but was defeated by Caesar's legate Gaius Fabius and fled. Under Rome their chief town was Juliomagus, later called Andecavi, the origin of Angers and of the name Anjou.

alba-longa.t: Legendary mother city of the Latins in the Alban Hills, remembered by the Romans as the home of Romulus and Remus and the seat of the Latin festival.
alba-longa.o: Roman tradition held that Ascanius, son of the Trojan hero Aeneas, founded Alba Longa about thirty years after Lavinium, and placed its foundation in the 12th century BCE. Archaeology shows Iron Age villages and cemeteries around the Alban Lake and Monte Cavo from about 1000 BCE, but no single city has been firmly identified.
alba-longa.r: The Romans described a line of Alban kings, from Silvius to Numitor and his usurping brother Amulius, but these are legendary. What is more secure is the role of the Alban Hills as a religious centre for the Latin peoples: the sanctuary of Jupiter Latiaris on Monte Cavo hosted the Feriae Latinae, a shared festival that Rome kept celebrating long after Alba disappeared.
alba-longa.e: According to Livy, Rome under Tullus Hostilius defeated Alba after the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii in the mid-7th century BCE, razed the city and moved its people to the Caelian Hill. Leading Roman families such as the Julii claimed Alban descent, and the Latin League inherited its religious role.

arcadian-league.t: Short-lived federation of the Arcadian cities created after Leuctra, which built Megalopolis and helped break Spartan power in the Peloponnese.
arcadian-league.o: Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE freed the Arcadians to act together. Led by Lycomedes of Mantinea and backed by Thebes, they formed a federal state in 370 BCE, and Mantinea was refounded. A new federal capital, Megalopolis, was built by uniting dozens of villages in south-western Arcadia.
arcadian-league.r: The league had an assembly known as the Ten Thousand, a federal council and magistrates, and a standing elite force, the eparitoi, paid from federal funds. It joined Thebes in invading Laconia and supported the refounding of Messene. Arcadian pride and a sense of common identity were expressed in federal coins and dedications.
arcadian-league.e: Quarrels with Elis led the Arcadians to seize Olympia, and disputes over using the sanctuary's treasure to pay the eparitoi split the league in 363 BCE, with Mantinea siding with Sparta and Tegea with Thebes. The Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE left the federation broken, though Megalopolis endured.

astures.t: The peoples of Asturias and León, last in Iberia to fall to Rome in 19 BCE, whose land became the empire's great gold-mining district.
astures.o: The Astures occupied the lands between the Cantabrian coast and the Douro, in modern Asturias, León and northern Zamora, from about the 4th century BCE. Romans divided them into the Transmontani north of the mountains and the Augustani on the plateau to the south.
astures.r: They lived in castros, fortified hilltop villages of round stone houses, in many independent communities grouped by kinship. Herding, farming and metalworking supported them, and their mountains held rich gold deposits. Their main stronghold on the plain was Lancia, near León. They spoke a Celtic language.
astures.e: The Astures fought alongside the Cantabri in Augustus' Cantabrian Wars of 29 to 19 BCE. After conquest Rome founded Asturica Augusta (Astorga) and exploited the gold of Las Médulas on a vast scale. Their name survives in Asturias and in the later Kingdom of Asturias.

ahhiyawa.t: A Late Bronze Age power named in some thirty Hittite texts, widely identified with the Mycenaean Greeks, the Achaeans of Homer.
ahhiyawa.o: The name Ahhiyawa, close to Homer's Achaeans, appears in Hittite records from c. 1400 BCE, when a 'man of Ahhiya' named Attarissiya raided western Anatolia and Alashiya. Most scholars now accept that it denotes a Mycenaean Greek kingdom, or a coalition of them, though its centre is debated, with Mycenae, Thebes and Rhodes all proposed.
ahhiyawa.r: In the 13th century BCE a Hittite king addressed the king of Ahhiyawa as a 'Great King' and 'brother', ranking him with Egypt, Babylon and Assyria. Ahhiyawa held Millawanda on the Anatolian coast and backed rebels such as Piyamaradu. Hittite texts mention ships from Ahhiyawa and a dispute over Wilusa, often linked with Troy.
ahhiyawa.e: In a treaty of Tudhaliya IV, c. 1230 BCE, the king of Ahhiyawa was struck from the list of great kings, suggesting its power had waned. References cease soon after, as the Mycenaean palaces collapsed c. 1200 BCE.

aedui.t: Leading people of central Gaul and Rome's oldest Gallic ally, whose quarrels with their rivals gave Caesar his pretext to invade Gaul.
aedui.o: The Aedui held the land between the Loire and the Saône, in modern Burgundy, with their great oppidum at Bibracte on Mont Beuvray. By the 2nd century BCE they were hailed by the Roman Senate as brothers and kinsmen of the Roman people, and they contested leadership of Gaul with the Arverni and the Sequani.
aedui.r: Government was oligarchic: a council of nobles and an annual chief magistrate, the vergobret, who could not leave the territory during office. Bibracte was a large town of craftsmen, enamellers and traders importing Italian wine. The druid Diviciacus spoke for Rome in the Senate, while his brother Dumnorix led the anti-Roman party.
aedui.e: Pressed by the Sequani and Ariovistus, the Aedui called on Caesar in 58 BCE, but in 52 BCE they joined Vercingetorix, who was chosen supreme leader at Bibracte. Pardoned after Alesia, they moved to the new city of Augustodunum (Autun), and in 48 CE Claudius admitted Aeduan nobles to the Roman Senate.

atrebates.t: Belgic people of Artois whose king Commius served Caesar, then turned against him and founded a dynasty in Britain.
atrebates.o: The Atrebates lived in the modern Artois around Nemetocenna (Arras). They joined the Belgic league in 57 BCE, promising fifteen thousand men, and fought beside the Nervii at the Sabis.
atrebates.r: After their defeat Caesar made Commius their king and used him as an envoy to the Britons in 55 BCE, extending his authority over the Morini. Their coins and their links across the Channel show close ties with Britain, where a people of the same name lived.
atrebates.e: Commius joined the great revolt of 52 BCE, helped lead the relief army at Alesia and later fled to Britain, where coins name his successors among the British Atrebates. Under Rome Nemetocenna became a civitas capital, the origin of Arras, and the name survives in Artois.

atrebates-britain.t: Southern British kingdom founded by the Gallic exile Commius, whose last king Verica fled to Rome and gave Claudius his pretext for invasion in 43.
atrebates-britain.o: Commius, king of the Atrebates of northern Gaul, first served Julius Caesar and then joined the Gallic revolt of 52 BCE. Around 50 BCE he fled across the Channel, and coins bearing his name soon appear in central southern Britain, where he appears to have founded a dynasty ruling Hampshire, Berkshire and Sussex.
atrebates-britain.r: Kings claiming descent from Commius, notably Tincomarus, Eppillus and Verica, issued gold coins that increasingly copied Roman designs, and Verica's carry a vine leaf and the title REX, signs of friendship with Rome. Calleva, the later Silchester, grew into a planned oppidum with imported wine, olive oil and tableware. Pressure from the Catuvellauni under Cunobelinus and his sons steadily shrank the kingdom.
atrebates-britain.e: Around 41 or 42 Verica was driven out and went to Rome to seek help, which Claudius used to justify the invasion of 43. Afterwards much of the territory passed to the client Kingdom of the Regni under Togidubnus, and Calleva Atrebatum became a civitas capital of Roman Britain.

aegina.t: Island state in the Saronic Gulf that minted some of the first Greek coins and was the great commercial rival of Athens until 431 BCE.
aegina.o: Aegina, an island between Attica and the Argolid, was settled from the Neolithic and had a strong Bronze Age town at Kolonna. In the early Iron Age it was resettled by Dorians from Epidaurus, and by the 7th century BCE it had become one of the busiest trading states of the Greek world.
aegina.r: Aegina struck silver 'turtle' coins from c. 550 BCE, and its weight standard spread across much of Greece. Its merchants traded at Naucratis in Egypt, and its oligarchic elite built the temple of Aphaia, whose pediment sculptures are now in Munich. Aegina gave earth and water to Persia in 491 BCE, but its ships won the prize for valour at Salamis in 480 BCE.
aegina.e: Long wars with Athens ended in 457 BCE, when Aegina was forced into the Delian League. In 431 BCE Athens expelled the Aeginetans and settled colonists; Sparta gave the exiles land at Thyrea. Lysander restored survivors in 405 BCE, but the island never regained its former power.

abrincatui.t: Small Gallic people of the bay of Mont Saint-Michel, whose name survives in the town of Avranches.
abrincatui.o: Known only from Pliny, Ptolemy and later Roman records, the Abrincatui held the southern end of the Cotentin coast on the border of Normandy and Brittany. They were neighbours of the Unelli and Redones and were probably dependents of a larger Armorican people.
abrincatui.r: Nothing is recorded of their institutions. Ptolemy names their town Ingena, generally placed at Avranches.
abrincatui.e: They were drawn into the Roman conquest of Armorica in 57 and 56 BCE. Under Rome they formed a small civitas in Gallia Lugdunensis whose chief town took the people's name as Abrincatae, the origin of Avranches, later a bishopric.

ausci.t: Aquitanian people of Gascony whose chief town Elimberris became Auch, later the religious capital of the region.
ausci.o: The Ausci lived in the hills of central Gascony, in the modern Gers. They were among the Aquitani, whose language was related to Basque; the name of their town, Elimberris, is usually read as Basque-like 'new town', comparable with Iliberris in Iberia.
ausci.r: Pomponius Mela calls them the most distinguished of the Aquitanian peoples. Nothing is recorded of their rulers before the conquest.
ausci.e: The Ausci gave hostages to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE without fighting. Their town was refounded as Augusta Auscorum and in late antiquity became the metropolis of the province of Novempopulana. Auch remained the seat of an archbishop for all of Gascony.

arretium.t: Northern Etruscan city, home of the bronze Chimera of Arezzo, which grew rich on farming and metalworking and became an early Roman ally.
arretium.o: Arretium, Etruscan Aritim, modern Arezzo, lay where the Val di Chiana meets the upper Arno, controlling routes between Etruria, Umbria and the Po valley. It developed into a city from the 6th century BCE, later than most Etruscan centres, and grew powerful in the 4th century BCE.
arretium.r: Arretium was known for agriculture and metalwork. The bronze Chimera of Arezzo, cast around 400 BCE and found in 1553, is a masterpiece of Etruscan art. The city was dominated by great families, among them the Cilnii, whom Livy reports being driven out by a popular revolt in 302 BCE and restored with Roman help; the Augustan minister Maecenas was descended from them.
arretium.e: Arretium made truces with Rome in 310 and 294 BCE and became a loyal ally, supplying weapons and grain to Scipio in 205 BCE. Under Rome it became famous for Arretine ware, a red-glazed tableware exported across the empire. The town continued as Arezzo, birthplace of Petrarch.

airenosi.t: A Pyrenean people known only from Polybius' list of those Hannibal conquered in 218 BCE, possibly of the Val d'Aran.
airenosi.o: The Airenosi appear in Polybius among the peoples between the Ebro and the Pyrenees subdued by Hannibal in 218 BCE. Their location is uncertain; they are often placed in the central Pyrenees, perhaps in the Val d'Aran, on the basis of their name.
airenosi.r: Nothing is known of their society or government.
airenosi.e: After Hannibal's conquest the region was held for Carthage by Hanno until the Roman advance. It came under Rome in the early 2nd century BCE, and the Airenosi disappear from the record.

arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.t: Nearly three centuries in which Cyprus was neutral ground shared between the Byzantine Empire and the Caliphate, which split its taxes.
arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.o: Arab fleets raided Cyprus from 649. In 688 the Byzantine emperor Justinian II and the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik agreed a treaty under which the revenues of Cyprus, along with those of Armenia and Iberia, were divided equally between them. The island was to be demilitarised and neutral, though the arrangement was repeatedly interrupted.
arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.r: Cyprus kept its Greek-speaking Christian population, its bishops and local officials, while paying tribute to both powers. Justinian II moved many islanders to Cyzicus around 691, and they returned about 698. Both sides violated the neutrality: Byzantine and Abbasid fleets raided the island, and Harun al-Rashid's forces deported Cypriots. Historians debate how formal the condominium really was.
arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.e: As Byzantine power revived in the 10th century, Nikephoros II Phokas sent the patrician Niketas Chalkoutzes to retake Cyprus in 965. It became a Byzantine province until Isaac Komnenos seized it in 1184.

aulerci-diablintes.t: Branch of the Aulerci in the western Mayenne whose Roman town at Jublains preserves one of the best surviving Roman forts in France.
aulerci-diablintes.o: The Aulerci were a group of related peoples in north-western Gaul; the Diablintes held the area around Jublains in Mayenne, between the Cenomani and the Redones. Caesar names them among the allies of the Veneti, and Ptolemy gives their town as Noviodunum.
aulerci-diablintes.r: Very little is known of their society before the conquest. They shared in the Atlantic and Armorican trade networks and struck coins of Armorican type.
aulerci-diablintes.e: After joining the Veneti in 56 BCE they were defeated and absorbed into Gallia Lugdunensis. Their Roman town of Noviodunum Diablintum at Jublains, with its temple, baths, theatre and fortified store-building, declined in late antiquity when the civitas merged with that of the Cenomani.

athens.t: The city-state of Attica that created democracy, led the Delian League and produced the drama, philosophy and architecture at the heart of Classical Greek culture.
athens.o: Athens was inhabited continuously from the Bronze Age, and the Acropolis held a Mycenaean palace. In the early Iron Age the communities of Attica were unified under Athens, a process the Greeks credited to Theseus. Kings gave way to annual archons drawn from the aristocracy, and the city adopted Draco's written laws in 621 BCE.
athens.r: Solon's reforms of 594 BCE ended debt bondage; Peisistratus then ruled as tyrant, and Cleisthenes founded democracy in 508 BCE. Athens defeated Persia at Marathon and Salamis, then led the Delian League. Under Pericles it built the Parthenon and staged the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, funded by silver from Laurion.
athens.e: Defeat by Sparta in 404 BCE ended its empire, though it led the Second Athenian League until Chaeronea in 338 BCE. Under Macedonian and Roman influence it remained a centre of philosophy. After it sided with Mithridates, Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BCE.

amphictyonic-league.t: Ancient religious association of Greek peoples that managed the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi and repeatedly declared sacred wars that drew in the great powers.
amphictyonic-league.o: An amphictyony was a league of neighbours sharing a sanctuary. This one began at the shrine of Demeter at Anthela near Thermopylae and extended its care to Delphi. Its role became prominent in the First Sacred War, traditionally c. 595-585 BCE, when members destroyed the town of Kirrha for abusing pilgrims and then reorganised the Pythian Games in 582 BCE.
amphictyonic-league.r: Twelve peoples, among them the Thessalians, Phocians, Boeotians, Dorians and Ionians, each sent two delegates (hieromnemones) to a council meeting twice a year at Anthela and Delphi. The council looked after temple property and finances, the Pythian Games and the sacred land, and could fine or declare war on offenders. Powerful states used its votes to dress political aims as piety.
amphictyonic-league.e: The Third Sacred War against Phocis (356-346 BCE) brought Philip II of Macedon onto the council, and the Fourth (339 BCE) led to his victory at Chaeronea. The Aetolian League dominated it in the 3rd century BCE. Augustus reorganised its membership, and it lingered as a religious body into the 2nd century CE.
amphictyonic-league.re: Ancient Greek religion (cult of Apollo and Demeter)

achaean-league.t: Federation of Peloponnesian cities that grew under Aratus and Philopoemen to unite the whole Peloponnese before its destruction by Rome in 146 BCE.
achaean-league.o: An older league of the small cities of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth had collapsed under Macedonian rule. In 280 BCE four cities, Dyme, Patrae, Tritaia and Pharai, refounded it. Aratus brought in Sicyon in 251 BCE and seized Acrocorinth from the Macedonians in 243 BCE, making the league a major power.
achaean-league.r: Members kept local government but shared citizenship, coinage, weights and foreign policy. Assemblies met at Aigion, electing an annual general (strategos), who could not serve consecutive terms. Polybius, himself an Achaean, praised it as a model of federal union. Under Philopoemen it absorbed Sparta, Messene and Elis, uniting the Peloponnese by 191 BCE.
achaean-league.e: War with Cleomenes III forced Aratus to invite back Macedon. Rome later used disputes over Sparta to intervene; in 146 BCE the league declared war, and Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth. The league was dissolved, revived later only as a minor body.

ancient-veneti.t: Iron Age people of north-eastern Italy, centred on Ateste and Patavium, famed for horse-breeding and bronze work, who became Rome's peaceful allies and gave their name to Venice.
ancient-veneti.o: The Veneti emerged in the plain between the Po, the Adige and the Alps in the early 1st millennium BCE, forming the Este culture from about 1000 BCE. Greek and Roman writers linked them to the Eneti of Paphlagonia or to Trojan refugees under Antenor, legends Padua later embraced, but archaeology shows a mainly local development.
ancient-veneti.r: Their main centres were Ateste (Este), Patavium (Padua), Vicetia and Altinum, each probably self-governing. They wrote Venetic, an Indo-European language, in an alphabet adapted from Etruscan, known from hundreds of votive inscriptions. Bronze situlae decorated with processions and banquets, amber trade from the Baltic, and celebrated horse-breeding marked their culture; the healing goddess Reitia had a major sanctuary at Este.
ancient-veneti.e: Hostile to the Gauls, the Veneti allied with Rome from the 3rd century BCE and were absorbed gradually and without conquest. Latin replaced Venetic, and Caesar's grant of citizenship in 49 BCE completed integration. Their name lived on in the Roman region of Venetia et Histria and, through it, in Venice and the Veneto.

abdera-800.t: A Phoenician trading port on the coast of Almería, at modern Adra, that later minted coins under Carthaginian and Roman rule.
abdera-800.o: Phoenician settlers founded Abdera in the 8th century BCE on the hill of Montecristo at modern Adra, at the mouth of the river Adra. It was one of a chain of Phoenician harbours along the southern coast of Iberia, with Sexi and Malaka, linking Gadir with the eastern Mediterranean.
abdera-800.r: Little is known of its government. Like its neighbours, Abdera lived from trade with the Iberian hinterland, fishing and the salting of fish. In the Punic period it fell under the influence of Carthage, and its later coins, inscribed in Punic letters, showed a temple facade with tuna fish.
abdera-800.e: After the Roman victory over Carthage in Hispania in 206 BCE Abdera came under Rome, keeping its coinage into the early empire. It continued as a small Roman town, and Strabo listed it among the Phoenician foundations of the coast.

auteini.t: People of western Ireland named by Ptolemy, usually placed in Galway or Mayo and possibly linked with the later Uaithni.
auteini.o: The Auteini, or Autini, are listed in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the west coast of Ireland, between the Nagnatae to the north and the Gangani (Ireland) to the south, roughly in modern Galway or Mayo. Ptolemy's Irish data came from earlier maritime reports and are imprecise.
auteini.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Their name is often compared with the Uaithni, a population group recorded in early medieval Ireland in north Tipperary and Limerick, which could indicate a later movement south or a mistaken placing by Ptolemy, but the identification remains conjecture.
auteini.e: The Auteini do not appear in later records. The west of Ireland where Ptolemy placed them later formed part of the Kingdom of Connacht.

albici.t: Hardy mountain people of upper Provence who fought for Massalia against Caesar's siege in 49 BCE.
albici.o: The Albici lived in the hills north of Massalia, probably around the plateau of Albion and the area of Riez, whose Roman name Alebaece Reiorum may preserve theirs. Caesar describes them as old clients of Massalia.
albici.r: Caesar calls them barbarians living in the mountains above Massilia, under the protection of the Greek city, and praises their courage. No rulers or institutions are recorded.
albici.e: In 49 BCE the Massaliots brought the Albici into the city as defenders against Caesar's legates, but the siege ended in surrender. Their land was then absorbed into Gallia Narbonensis.

autrigones.t: A people of northern Burgos and western Bizkaia, whose towns Virovesca and Flaviobriga linked the Meseta to the Cantabrian Sea.
autrigones.o: The Autrigones occupied the land from the upper Ebro to the coast around Castro Urdiales, in modern Burgos, Álava and Bizkaia, from the later Iron Age. They bordered the Cantabri, Turmodigi, Caristii and Berones, and their language was probably Celtic.
autrigones.r: They lived in hillforts and lowland settlements, farming and herding, with towns such as Virovesca (Briviesca) and Tritium Autrigonum named by Pliny and Ptolemy. Their political organisation is unknown.
autrigones.e: They came under Rome during the 1st century BCE, and after the Cantabrian Wars their territory became part of Hispania Tarraconensis. The Flavian emperors founded the port of Flaviobriga on their coast, modern Castro Urdiales.

alderney.t: The northernmost of the inhabited Channel Islands, a self-governing part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey with its own States and a long history as a fortress.
alderney.o: Alderney was part of the Duchy of Normandy and stayed loyal to the English crown when King John lost mainland Normandy to France in 1204. Like the other Channel Islands it remained a possession of the crown in its role as Duke of Normandy, never part of the Kingdom of England.
alderney.r: The island was governed under Norman customary law, and from 1584 to 1825 held by hereditary governors. The British built a chain of Victorian forts and the breakwater at Braye. During the German occupation of 1940 to 1945 the population was evacuated and the Nazis built labour camps there.
alderney.e: Alderney's residents returned in 1945. Since 1949 it has been part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey for some matters, while keeping its own elected States of Alderney, and remains a British Crown Dependency.

ausetani.t: An Iberian people of the plain of Vic in Catalonia, whose name survives in the later County of Osona.
ausetani.o: The Ausetani lived on the plain of Vic and the surrounding hills in central Catalonia from about the 5th century BCE. Their chief town was Ausa, on the site of modern Vic, and the fortified settlement of L'Esquerda lay nearby.
ausetani.r: Little is known of their institutions beyond Livy's narrative. They lived from farming and herding, and minted coins with the Iberian legend Ausesken. During the Second Punic War they sided with Carthage, and their leader Amusicus fled to Hasdrubal when the Romans besieged their town for thirty days.
ausetani.e: After further resistance during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE, they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior. Ausa became the Roman town of Ausa, later Vicus Ausonensis, and their name lived on in the medieval County of Osona.

allobroges.t: Powerful Gallic people between the Rhône and the Isère, conquered by Rome in 121 BCE, whose envoys exposed the Catilinarian conspiracy.
allobroges.o: The Allobroges held the land between the Rhône, the Isère and Lake Geneva, in the modern Isère and Savoy. Their chief town was Vienna (Vienne), and Genava (Geneva) stood on their northern border. Livy notes them on Hannibal's route through the Alps in 218 BCE.
allobroges.r: They were a warlike people governed by a nobility, rich in cattle and controlling routes into the Alps. In 123 BCE they sheltered Teutomalius, king of the Salyes, which gave Rome its pretext for war.
allobroges.e: Rome defeated them in 121 BCE, and their land became part of Gallia Narbonensis. In 63 BCE their envoys revealed Catiline's plot to Cicero, but in 61 BCE they rose under Catugnatus and were crushed. Vienne became a wealthy Roman colony.

arverni.t: Leading people of central Gaul, rulers of the Auvergne, whose noble Vercingetorix united Gaul against Caesar in 52 BCE.
arverni.o: The Arverni held the volcanic uplands and the fertile Limagne plain of the Auvergne. By the 2nd century BCE they dominated much of southern and central Gaul. Their king Luernios was remembered by Greek writers for scattering gold and silver to his followers, and his son Bituitus led a vast army against Rome.
arverni.r: Their power rested on a network of client peoples, such as the Gabali, Vellavi and Cadurci, and on great oppida like Corent and Gergovia, which imported Italian wine on a huge scale. After the defeat of Bituitus kingship was abolished, and Celtillus, father of Vercingetorix, was put to death for seeking to restore it.
arverni.e: Bituitus was defeated by the Roman Republic in 121 BCE. In 52 BCE Vercingetorix raised Gaul in revolt and repulsed Caesar at Gergovia, but surrendered at Alesia and was later executed in Rome. The Arverni were treated leniently, and their Roman capital Augustonemetum grew into Clermont-Ferrand.

aulerci-eburovices.t: Branch of the Aulerci around Évreux in Normandy who killed their own council rather than stay out of the war against Caesar.
aulerci-eburovices.o: The Eburovices were part of the Aulerci group of peoples and held the land between the Seine and the Eure, around the oppidum later called Mediolanum Aulercorum.
aulerci-eburovices.r: Caesar records that in 56 BCE they and the Lexovii murdered their senators, who opposed war, and joined the coalition of Viridovix of the Unelli. The episode shows that they were governed by a council of nobles.
aulerci-eburovices.e: The coalition was defeated by Quintus Titurius Sabinus in 56 BCE, and the Eburovices joined the general revolt again in 52 BCE. Under Rome Mediolanum Aulercorum became a civitas capital, the origin of Évreux.

antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.t: Macedon under Cassander, son of Antipater, who ended Alexander the Great's line, founded Thessalonica and briefly passed the throne to his sons.
antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.o: After the regent Antipater died in 319 BCE, his son Cassander fought Polyperchon and Olympias for Macedon and won control by 316 BCE, executing Olympias. He married Alexander's half-sister Thessalonike. Around 310 BCE he had Alexander IV and his mother Roxane killed, and in 305 BCE took the title of king.
antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.r: Cassander ruled from Pella with the support of the Macedonian aristocracy, controlling much of Greece through garrisons and friendly governments, such as that of Demetrius of Phalerum at Athens. He refounded Thebes and founded Thessalonica and Cassandreia, the latter on the site of Potidaea. He was an ally of Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy against Antigonus I.
antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.e: Cassander died in 297 BCE. His son Philip IV died soon after, and the brothers Antipater II and Alexander V fought over the throne. Demetrius Poliorcetes, called in by Alexander V, murdered him in 294 BCE and took Macedon, ending the dynasty and opening the way for the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia.

andosini.t: A Pyrenean people subdued by Hannibal on his march to Italy in 218 BCE, often linked with the name of Andorra.
andosini.o: The Andosini are known only from Polybius, who lists them among the peoples between the Ebro and the Pyrenees that Hannibal conquered in 218 BCE. They are usually placed in the high valleys around modern Andorra, whose name is often thought to derive from theirs.
andosini.r: Nothing is known of their society beyond a probable mountain economy of herding and small-scale farming.
andosini.e: After Hannibal's campaign their territory was left under the Carthaginian officer Hanno. Following the Roman victories in the north-east and Cato's campaign of 195 BCE, the area passed into Hispania Citerior, and the Andosini are not mentioned again.

amphipolis.t: Athenian colony on the Strymon river, key to the timber and gold of Thrace, whose loss to Sparta in 424 BCE exiled the historian Thucydides.
amphipolis.o: The site, a loop of the lower Strymon called Ennea Hodoi (Nine Ways), had long attracted Athens; a first attempt to settle it ended in disaster around 465 BCE. In 437 BCE Hagnon founded Amphipolis there with Athenian and allied settlers, controlling the river crossing and the route to the timber and gold and silver mines of Mount Pangaion.
amphipolis.r: Amphipolis was a mixed community in which Athenians were a minority among other Greek settlers, which weakened loyalty to Athens. It governed itself through an assembly and magistrates, honoured Hagnon as founder and later the Spartan Brasidas, and grew rich on timber for shipbuilding, precious metals and trade with Thrace and Macedon.
amphipolis.e: Brasidas captured it in 424 BCE; both he and the Athenian Cleon died in battle there in 422 BCE. Independent afterwards and never recovered by Athens, it fell to Philip II in 357 BCE. It became a leading Macedonian city and mint, and in 167 BCE capital of one of the Four Macedonian Republics.

ambarri.t: Gallic people of the lower Saône and Ain, clients of the Aedui whose appeal for help helped draw Caesar into Gaul in 58 BCE.
ambarri.o: Their name means those on both sides of the Arar, the ancient Saône. Livy lists the Ambarri among the peoples who followed Bellovesus into northern Italy in the legendary migrations of around 600 BCE. In Caesar's day they lived east of the Saône, near the Rhône confluence.
ambarri.r: Caesar calls them friends and kinsmen of the Aedui, on whom they depended. No rulers or towns are recorded.
ambarri.e: When the migrating Helvetii plundered their fields in 58 BCE, the Ambarri complained to Caesar, adding to his reasons to attack. After the conquest their territory was divided among neighbouring civitates, and the name survives only in a few place names in the Ain.

ambiani.t: Belgic people of the Somme valley whose town Samarobriva, modern Amiens, hosted Caesar's council of Gaul in 54 BCE.
ambiani.o: The Ambiani held the lower and middle Somme in Picardy. Caesar records that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE and surrendered after the league broke up.
ambiani.r: Their oppidum of Samarobriva, the bridge on the Samara or Somme, controlled a key crossing. They struck abundant gold coins, some of the earliest in northern Gaul.
ambiani.e: Caesar held an assembly of the Gallic peoples at Samarobriva in 54 BCE and wintered there. The Ambiani sent men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE and fought again in 51 BCE. Under Rome Samarobriva became a major city, later Ambianum, the origin of Amiens.

aetolian-league.t: Federal state of the Aetolians of west-central Greece that became one of the great powers of Hellenistic Greece and controlled the oracle of Delphi.
aetolian-league.o: The Aetolians lived in mountain villages north of the Gulf of Corinth, scorned by Thucydides as primitive. By 367 BCE an Aetolian federation was acting as a state, with its religious centre at the sanctuary of Apollo at Thermon. Its prestige soared when it helped repel the Gallic invasion of Delphi in 279 BCE.
aetolian-league.r: The league had a general assembly of all citizens meeting at Thermon and elsewhere, a large council and an annual general (strategos) assisted by a committee, the apokletoi. It expanded by granting citizenship or alliance to distant cities, controlled the votes of the Amphictyonic League and was notorious for licensed raiding and piracy. Leaders such as Dorimachus and Scopas fought Philip V of Macedon.
aetolian-league.e: Allied with Rome against Philip V in 211 BCE, the Aetolians felt cheated after Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE and invited Antiochus III to Greece. Defeated at Thermopylae in 191 BCE, the league accepted a peace in 189 BCE that left it a subordinate ally of Rome.

arevaci.t: The strongest of the Celtiberian peoples, defenders of Numantia, whose siege by Scipio Aemilianus in 134 to 133 BCE became a byword for resistance.
arevaci.o: The Arevaci occupied the upper Douro basin in modern Soria and Segovia from about the 4th century BCE. Strabo called them the most powerful of the Celtiberians, and their towns included Numantia, Termes and Uxama.
arevaci.r: They lived in large fortified towns with grid-like streets, governed by councils and elected war leaders. Numantia's pottery shows painted horses and warriors. Herding, cereal growing and iron working sustained them, and their warriors were renowned in Roman sources for courage and skill with the sword.
arevaci.e: From 153 BCE they led resistance to Rome, defeating several consuls. In 134 BCE Scipio Aemilianus surrounded Numantia with walls and starved it; Retogenes broke out to seek aid, but the town fell in 133 BCE. The Arevaci later backed Sertorius before becoming part of Hispania Citerior.

acarnanian-league.t: Federation of the Acarnanian towns of western Greece, a long-standing enemy of the Aetolians and an ally first of Athens and later of Macedon.
acarnanian-league.o: Acarnania, between the Ambracian Gulf and the Achelous river, was a land of small towns and villages. By the mid-5th century BCE they were acting together as a league with its meeting place at Stratos. Hostility to Corinth's colonies in the region pushed them into alliance with Athens, whose general Phormio campaigned with them in the Peloponnesian War.
acarnanian-league.r: The league had a federal assembly, council and elected general (strategos), and struck federal coins. Its members were mainly farmers and herders known as skilled slingers and fighters. Ancient writers considered the Acarnanians conservative and fiercely loyal to allies, especially in their long struggle against the expanding Aetolian League.
acarnanian-league.e: Aetolia and Epirus partitioned Acarnania in the mid-3rd century BCE, but the league was restored around 230 BCE and sided with Macedon. Rome detached Leucas and made it the federal capital in 197 BCE. The league faded under Roman rule; after Actium in 31 BCE Augustus moved much of its population to his new city of Nicopolis.

ancalites.t: British people named once by Julius Caesar among those who surrendered to him in 54 BCE, leading him to the stronghold of Cassivellaunus.
ancalites.o: The Ancalites are known only from Caesar's Gallic War. In 54 BCE they were among five British peoples, alongside the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Bibroci and Cassi, who sent embassies to submit after the Trinovantes had won his protection.
ancalites.r: Caesar says that from these envoys he learned the location of Cassivellaunus's stronghold, protected by woods and marshes, which he then stormed. Beyond this, nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs, and their territory is uncertain, though the upper Thames valley has been suggested.
ancalites.e: No later source mentions the Ancalites. They were probably absorbed by stronger neighbours such as the Catuvellauni or the Atrebates (Britain) in the century before the Roman conquest of 43.

aulerci-cenomani.t: Gallic people of Maine, centred on Le Mans, a branch of whom crossed the Alps and founded the Celtic towns of Brescia and Verona.
aulerci-cenomani.o: The Cenomani were the largest branch of the Aulerci and held the Sarthe valley around Vindinum (Le Mans). Livy and Polybius report that part of the people migrated across the Alps around 400 BCE and settled north of the Po, where the Italian Cenomani founded Brixia (Brescia) and became allies of Rome against the other Gauls.
aulerci-cenomani.r: Little is known of the Gallic Cenomani at home. They struck gold coins and controlled the route between the Loire and the Channel coast.
aulerci-cenomani.e: They joined the great revolt of 52 BCE and sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia. Under Rome Vindinum grew into a walled town, later called Civitas Cenomanorum, from which come the names Le Mans and Maine.

cr.a: Cénomans (peuple celtique de Gaule). Autorité émettrice de monnaie

antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.t: Kingdom of the Antigonid dynasty, which ruled Macedon and dominated Greece for over a century until defeated by Rome at Pydna in 168 BCE.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.o: Antigonus I Monophthalmus and his son Demetrius Poliorcetes, generals of Alexander, took the royal title in 306 BCE while ruling in Asia. Demetrius seized Macedon in 294 BCE but lost it in 288 BCE. His son Antigonus II Gonatas won the throne after defeating the Gauls at Lysimachia in 277 BCE, founding a stable dynasty at Pella.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.r: Antigonid kings ruled Macedon directly through a landed aristocracy and a citizen army famous for its sarissa phalanx, while controlling Greece through garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, the 'fetters of Greece'. They patronised philosophy and the arts. Antigonus III Doson formed a Hellenic alliance and defeated Sparta at Sellasia in 222 BCE.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.e: Philip V's alliance with Hannibal led to wars with Rome; defeat at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE confined him to Macedon. His son Perseus lost to Lucius Aemilius Paullus at Pydna in 168 BCE. Rome abolished the monarchy and divided the land into the Four Macedonian Republics.

aurunci.t: Ancient Italic people of the coast between Latium and Campania, whose towns were destroyed by Rome in 314 BCE.
aurunci.o: The Aurunci, called Ausones by the Greeks, lived between the Liri and Volturno rivers around the Roccamonfina volcano. Greek writers used 'Ausonia' for much of early Italy, which suggests they were once a widespread people. Little is known of their origins or language.
aurunci.r: Known only from Roman and Greek sources, the Aurunci lived in hill towns such as Ausona, Minturnae, Vescia and Suessa Aurunca. They fought Rome and the Latins in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, and later allied with the Sidicini against the Samnites.
aurunci.e: After they joined Rome's enemies during the Samnite Wars, Rome destroyed the towns of Ausona, Minturnae and Vescia in 314 BCE, massacring much of the population. Roman colonies followed at Suessa Aurunca in 313 BCE and Minturnae in 296 BCE, and the people disappeared from history.
